title: George Fox and the Quakers
hookLine: a shoemaker's apprentice hears there is one, even Christ Jesus, who can speak to your condition

cards: A young man in England has been put to work with a shoemaker. Something inside him is restless, and he walks from minister to minister with his questions.
In his journal he remembers one telling him, more or less, to take up tobacco and sing psalms. Another, he says, got angry when he stepped on the edge of a flower bed. Nobody can reach him.
He wanders, fasts, walks alone in the fields with his Bible. His name is George Fox, and what happens next starts a movement that sits down together in silence.

teach.h: A VOICE WHEN HOPE RAN OUT.

teach.b: When all his hopes in other people were gone, and nothing outside himself could help, he heard a voice that said, in his journal's words, "There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition."
And then: "my heart did leap for joy." The voice doesn't hand him a new argument or a better minister.
It says someone can speak to his condition: not the human condition in general, but his own, the exact shape of his restlessness.
Fox came to believe the light of Christ could reach any person directly, a shoemaker as much as a scholar, a woman as much as a man.
The people who gathered around him called themselves Friends. Others called them Quakers, and the name stuck.
In a traditional Quaker meeting, people sit together in silence, with no set sermon. If someone feels moved to speak, they stand and speak, briefly, and the quiet returns. The silence isn't empty.
It's waiting. There's an old story behind that kind of waiting. The prophet Elijah stands on a mountain.
A wind tears at the rocks, but God is not in the wind. Then an earthquake, then a fire, and God is not in them either. And after the fire, in the King James words, "a still small voice."
Friends sit down expecting that voice could come to anyone in the room. Other Christians pray with set words, music and liturgy, and they too speak of God meeting them there.

how: In a traditional Quaker meeting for worship, Friends sit together in silence with no set sermon, and anyone who feels moved may stand and speak briefly before the silence returns.

games.q: you're George Fox. you've asked minister after minister, and nobody can help. what now?
o: keep searching until you find the right preacher.
games.why: when all his hopes in people were gone, Fox heard a voice: there is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition.

practice: Sit the way Friends sit, as if something might be said: not clearing your mind, not making anything happen, hands resting, letting the sounds in the room pass.
If you pray, hold Fox's words loosely: someone can speak to my condition. If you don't, simply wait, and notice what rises in the quiet without chasing it.

wordCard.voice: Quakers. The name given to George Fox's Friends, who gathered to wait together in silence for the light of Christ to speak to each person directly.
